# Roadmap — V2 Candidates

**Status:** Parked. Nothing here is committed to. Revisit only after V1 is finished and
running unattended.

**Date parked:** 2026-07-28

---

## Why this file exists

Ideas generated while building V1 that were deliberately *not* pursued, so they don't get
lost and don't quietly expand V1's scope.

Each entry records what it is, why it might be worth doing, what it costs, and what the
risk is. Nothing is designed here — a spec gets written only if an item is actually chosen.

---

## The rule these were generated by

**Expand the LLM's role wherever the input is unstructured language and the output is
checkable. Nowhere else.**

That rule produced everything already built, and it rejects the tempting ideas — letting
the model rank severity, compute figures, or predict anything.

---

## Candidates

### 1. Questions for management

Given a filing's observations and findings, generate the three questions an analyst would
put to management on the earnings call.

**Why it's interesting:** a question makes no claim. *"Why did inventory grow 34% while
revenue grew 11%?"* asserts nothing — it points at a juxtaposition already verified. The
entire fabrication-risk apparatus built for SPEC-007 is unnecessary here, because there is
no proposition that can be false.

**Cost:** ~$0.02 per filing. **Risk:** very low. **Effort:** small — reuses SPEC-007's
selection and reference machinery unchanged.

Probably the best value-per-risk item on this list.

### 2. Year-over-year note diffing, explained

The observations layer detects *that* a note changed materially. It cannot say *what*
changed in meaning. Supply both versions and ask what substantively differs.

**Why it's interesting:** highest analytical ceiling of anything here. Comparing two texts
is exactly what language models are reliable at, and reading what changed in a footnote
year-over-year is exactly what analysts do.

**Bound it** to notes that matter — Debt, Income Taxes, Commitments and Contingencies,
Segment Information, Government Incentives — and only where the similarity check already
fired. Roughly 15–20 diffs.

**Cost:** ~$1. **Risk:** moderate, mitigated because output can be quote-anchored to the
new version, so SPEC-006's verification applies unchanged. **Effort:** medium.

### 3. Cross-company themes

One call per quarter over all three companies' findings: what appears in more than one?

**Why it's interesting:** for this specific watchlist it isn't decorative. Micron's HBM
feeds NVIDIA; Amazon buys from both. Export controls, AI capex and memory supply are
genuinely shared themes.

**Cost:** ~$0.02 per quarter. **Risk:** low — findings are already verified. **Effort:** small.

### 4. Plain-English note explainers

*"What is a valuation allowance and why does it matter?"* Written once per note **type**,
not per company. Cached permanently.

**Why it's interesting:** directly serves the requirement that the dashboard not intimidate
a non-specialist, without touching any company-specific claim.

**Cost:** ~20 explainers, trivial and one-off. **Risk:** very low — generic education, no
company facts. **Effort:** small.

### 5. Narrative continuity across quarters

*"Last quarter's brief flagged rising inventory; this quarter it has reversed."* Takes
prior briefs as input.

**Why it's interesting:** this is the "historical company memory" named in the project's
original brief and not yet built. It's also the thing a one-off summariser structurally
cannot do — it only exists because every filing was kept and analysed.

**Cost:** low — briefs are compact. **Risk:** low. **Effort:** small to medium.

### 6. Guidance tracking

Extract numeric guidance from 8-K Exhibit 99.1, compare to what was actually reported the
following quarter, and build a management credibility record.

**Why it's interesting:** the most institutional idea in the project. All three companies
give hard numeric guidance, so it's tractable rather than aspirational. Clean division of
labour — the model reads the press release, Python does the comparison.

**Cost:** low. **Risk:** low. **Effort:** medium, and **depends on Exhibit 99.1 extraction**
(SPEC-008 or later).

## SPEC-007 v2 prompt improvements

Found reviewing the first two real AC12 briefs (Amazon's and Micron's most recent 10-Ks,
2026-07-30) — real weaknesses in the GENERATOR's prompt, not in the verification machinery,
which caught nothing wrong here because nothing here is wrong: every sentence below is
accurate and grounded. This is about which TRUE, VERIFIED sentences get written, not about
fabrication. Parked rather than fixed immediately for the same reason as everything else in
this file — not designed until actually picked up. **Binding constraint on any future attempt
at either item: it must raise the connective share (juxtaposition/grouping over restatement)
without loosening a single R4/R5 verification constraint.** A prompt change that produces
more connected sentences by relaxing what gets checked is not an improvement.

1. **Prefer cross-type pairings for juxtaposition — an observation with a finding, or a
   metric with a section — over structural-to-structural.** Amazon's brief paired two
   `section_wording_changed`/`section_length_change` observations about the SAME note
   (near-tautological: a note that grew 73% longer is necessarily going to read as less
   similar to what it replaced) and, separately, paired the length of one note with the
   wording similarity of an entirely unrelated note (arbitrary — connected only by both
   surviving R2's selection, not by any real relationship between them). Micron's best
   juxtaposition, by contrast, connected a note's length change to the substantive
   litigation finding actually driving it (the Contingencies note growing 25% longer,
   paired with the $445M Netlist verdict behind it) — real, informative, and not
   coincidental. The fix is a prompt-level PREFERENCE, never a mechanical requirement
   (same-type pairings can be genuinely meaningful too, as Micron's SG&A/days-payables
   juxtaposition shows) — nothing for R4 to enforce here.

2. **Related restatements should merge into one sentence, not stay separate.** Amazon's
   brief listed the shortened server useful life ($1.0B), the store-impairment charge
   ($1.3B), and severance costs ($2.7B) as three independent restatements when they are one
   theme — three distinct charges that reduced 2025 earnings. Likewise, gross margin and
   operating margin both reaching 6-year highs in the same period were reported as two
   restatements rather than one. This is exactly what JUXTAPOSITION (or AGGREGATION, for a
   themed total) already exists to do — the fix is prompting the generator to reach for
   those types more often, not a new sentence type or a relaxed check.

Both point the same direction: the real run's restatement/juxtaposition/grouping mix
(70%/19%/10%) should shift toward more of the latter two, entirely at the generator-prompt
level — R4/R5 already accept everything a better-tuned generator would produce; nothing
about verification needs to change for either fix.

---

## Explicitly rejected

| Idea | Why not |
|---|---|
| AI-driven severity or ranking | Deliberately moved to Python in SPEC-005. Moving it back undoes the layer that makes everything else trustworthy. |
| Natural-language search over findings | Keyword matching does this for free. Don't pay a model to match strings. |
| Anything predictive | "This suggests margins will compress" is the one thing that cannot be made safe, and the thing most damaging to the project's credibility. |
| Earnings call transcripts | No free, reliable, legally clean machine-readable source. An availability wall, not a technical one. |
| Altman Z-score | Computes fine, tells you nothing for three investment-grade companies with large cash balances. |

---

## If revisiting

Suggested order, cheapest and safest first: **1, 4, 3, 5**, then **2**, then **6** once
Exhibit 99.1 extraction exists.

Total for the first four: under $0.50. Item 2 adds roughly $1.

None of this is expensive. The expensive layer — 273 footnotes analysed and verified — is
already built and paid for.
